extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty), journal editors, referees, and hiring committees — especially in combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on which mathematical results to write up and publish, how to judge others' publications, and how publication practices affect career development and community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish only work that fits your narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: If your little paper fits the narrative, do write it and publish it. If it helps you tell a good story — that sounds great. But if it’s a one-off thing, like you thought for some reason that you could solve a major open problem in another area — why tell anyone?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a paper helps you build a coherent research story that you can present in a job/colloquium talk. Prefer publishing pieces that contribute to an overarching program or narrative you can explain; avoid scattering one-off results that dilute your research identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of papers that make a good job talk — major-solution
rubrics_metrics.description: You can solve a major open problem. The talk writes itself then. You discuss the background, many famous people’s attempts and partial solutions. Then state your result and give an idea of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definitive breakthrough paper is the clearest route to a strong job/colloquium presentation — publish when you genuinely solve a major problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of papers that make a good job talk — coherent series
rubrics_metrics.description: You can tell a good story. … You start your talk by telling what’s the state of the sub-area, what are the major open problems and how do different aspects of your work fit in the picture. Then talk about how the technology that you develop over several papers positioned you to make a major advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer producing a sequence of related papers that develop tools and lead naturally to important results — this 'series' model is analogous to an artist’s recognizable series and is highly valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of papers that make a good job talk — small-result+presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: You can prove something small and nice, but be an amazing lecturer. You mesmerize the audience with your eloquence. For about 5 minutes after your talk they will keep thinking this little problem you solved is the most important result in all of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can present a modest result exceptionally well and engage audiences, a small paper can have outsized career benefit. Consider whether your presentation skills can amplify a small technical contribution before deciding to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge researchers by publication counts alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers rule the world — number of papers, citations, the h-index — but these measures can be misleading and manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using raw counts as proxy for quality. Investigate provenance of high counts (coauthorship patterns, venue selectivity). Numbers are informative but must be supplemented by qualitative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-inflation practices to watch for (form a clique)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Form a clique. Over the years build a group of 5-8 close collaborators. Keep writing papers in different subsets of 3-5 of them. Make sure each paper cites heavily all other subsets from the clique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a quantitative strategy to inflate apparent productivity. The author notes it is not necessarily flagged as unethical by major bodies but is abusive and detrimental; do not emulate. When evaluating authors, look for such clique patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-inflation practices to watch for (form a cartel)
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) Form a cartel. Invent an area and call yourselves collaborative research in that area. Apply for grants, organize conferences, publish proceedings, monographs, start your own journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates an appearance of legitimacy and inflates metrics. Treat such coordinated ecosystems skeptically when assessing impact; check independence and external validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-inflation practices to watch for (publish in low-quality/shady journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: (c) Publish in little known, not very selective or shady journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing widely in low-selectivity venues can inflate numbers but reduces signal quality. When judging candidates, account for venue selectivity and indexing (e.g., whether journal appears in MathSciNet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-inflation practices to watch for (organize special issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: (d) Organize special issues with these journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special issues can be vehicles for coordinated self-publishing. Consider editorial relationships and independence when evaluating such output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication-inflation practices to watch for (become an editor)
rubrics_metrics.description: (e) Become an editor of an established but not well managed journal and publish a lot there with all your collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial control can be abused to publish many related papers. Verify editorial practices and peer review integrity when assessing such publication records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-knowledge publishing (fraudulent pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A borderline-unethical strategy: create many papers proving equivalences among many statements surrounding a target conjecture, publish many correct-looking but weak/opaque reductions and some incorrect supporting papers, then announce a final reduction that (appears to) complete the proof based on previously accepted but shaky literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to patterns of many interlinked but low-quality or opaque papers that collectively claim a grand result. This can take years to be discovered; editors and referees should be skeptical of dispersed, barely-readable chains of equivalences and seek independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When judging others’ papers supplement content with author history
rubrics_metrics.description: First, read the paper, make a judgement on the validity and relative importance of the result. But then you supplement the judgement with what you know about the author, just like when you judge a painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider an author's publication record, prior reception, and reputation as additional signal. Examples: repetitive self-citation patterns or numerous similar short papers by same author may reduce confidence in novelty or discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess discoverability and utility for short/technical contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an editor sees a short bijective proof of a binomial identity but the author has many similar papers with mostly self-citations, then it's hard to check if the work was done before and whether future users will find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the contribution will be discoverable and useful to others (searchability, distinctiveness). If not, question the value added by publication even if the result is correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring/postdoc selection should match institutional goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Candidate A has 15 papers across diverse topics; Candidate B has 5 focused papers building a theory. Which to hire depends on what you need (independent collaborator vs someone to work closely building a program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align hiring choices with expected mentoring structure and institutional priorities. Broad publication records may favor institutions expecting independence; focused records suit close mentorship and long-term program-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid referees from the authors' clique
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are an editor and you see lots of repeated names among the authors' previous papers, it may be a clique. Make sure your referees are not from this clique, completely unrelated to them in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select referees with no close collaborative ties to authors to avoid bias. Check authors' coauthor networks when choosing referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suspicious of parallel/piecemeal papers claiming progress on big conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author has several parallel papers which prove not exactly related results towards the same goal, this might be a zero-knowledge publishing attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims advancing a major conjecture, scrutinize the coherence and independence of the evidence. If many fragmented papers are used to piece together a major claim, demand a definitive, verifiable consolidation.
